subject: Anthropology
title: The Potlatch
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Potlatch.

hook.text: A chief gives away everything — blankets, canoes, food — to hundreds of guests. He gains power by losing wealth.

buildup.text: The potlatch is a ceremonial feast among Northwest Coast peoples where hosts display status by giving away goods.

discovery.text: The more you give, the higher your rank. Rivals must match or exceed the gift, creating escalating cycles of generosity.

twist.text: Colonial rulers banned the potlatch, calling it wasteful. They couldn't grasp an economy based on giving, not keeping.

climax.text: The potlatch proves that wealth can flow outward. Status through generosity challenges the logic of accumulation.

punchline.text: In some economies, giving is gaining.

quiz.question: How does the potlatch determine social status?
options: By how much wealth you keep
By how much you give away to others

details.summary: The potlatch is a ceremonial feast among Northwest Coast peoples where hosts demonstrate status through competitive giving and even destruction of wealth. It functions as a redistributive system, a status competition, and a mechanism for recording social obligations and ranks.
details.whyItMatters: The potlatch overturns Western economic assumptions by showing that giving away wealth, not accumulating it, can be the highest form of economic achievement. It demonstrates that prestige economies operate on fundamentally different logic.
takeaways: Potlatch hosts gain status through competitive generosity
It functions as redistribution, status competition, and record-keeping
It demonstrates that prestige can come from giving, not accumulating

faq.question: Why would destroying wealth increase your status?
faq.answer: Destroying wealth demonstrates that you have so much that loss is insignificant — the ultimate display of power and abundance. Rivals must match or exceed the destruction or accept lower rank. The logic parallels conspicuous consumption but inverts accumulation into ostentatious disposal.

faq.question: What happened when potlatch was banned?
faq.answer: Canada banned the potlatch from 1884 to 1951 as part of forced assimilation. Ceremonial objects were confiscated and participants imprisoned. The ban disrupted social structures that depended on potlatch to distribute resources and establish rank. Communities continued practicing in secret.
